summary: Defines how to use AES-GCM authenticated encryption to provide confidentiality and data authentication in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol.

eli5.summary: This is a way to scramble audio and video in calls and check that nobody changed them, all in one step.

questions: how does aes-gcm work in srtp
how is the srtp iv formed for aes-gcm
why must the srtp authentication tag be 16 octets
subtitle: How to encrypt and authenticate SRTP and SRTCP packets in a single step using AES-GCM.

tldr.problem: SRTP protects real-time media with separate encryption and authentication steps. An authenticated-encryption cipher can do both at once, but SRTP needed rules for how to feed packets to it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two AES-GCM suites, AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM, each with a full 16-octet tag. It builds a 12-octet IV from the SSRC, packet index and a salt, and says which packet fields are encrypted, only authenticated, or left alone.
tldr.outcome: AES-GCM becomes a defined cipher for SRTP and SRTCP, with registrations for SDES, DTLS-SRTP and MIKEY. Reusing an IV is catastrophic, so the RFC requires strict counter and SSRC management and a rekey before any counter wraps.

today: RFC 7714 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 3711 with AES-GCM.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) is a profile of RTP that provides confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection for RTP traffic and for RTCP, the control traffic. Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) encrypts some data and also checks the integrity of both the encrypted data and some extra data that stays in the clear, called Associated Data.

This RFC defines how AES-GCM, a family of AEAD algorithms built on AES, is used in SRTP and SRTCP. It uses the generic AEAD interface of RFC 5116 and the AES versions with 128-bit and 256-bit keys.

Unlike some other protocols, the authentication tag MUST NOT be truncated: it MUST be a full 16 octets. That gives two configurations, AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM. The key size is set when the session starts and SHOULD NOT be changed.
sections.eli5: One box does two jobs: it hides what is inside and it carries a seal that shows if anyone touched it. The seal is always full-sized.

sections.title: The AEAD Security Architecture
sections.content:
Privacy and authentication both rely on symmetric algorithms, and AES-GCM combines them into one process. All endpoints share a secret master key, and a master key MAY be used by several endpoints that originate packets.

A key derivation function (KDF) turns the master key into separate keys for SRTP and SRTCP, as described in Section 4.3 of RFC 3711. The master key MUST be at least as large as the encryption key derived from it. Because AEAD merges encryption and authentication, no separate authentication keys are used.

How the master key is established, and how a session is rekeyed, are outside the scope of this document. The only related work is IANA registrations for SDES, DTLS-SRTP and MIKEY. Each endpoint needs two instantiations of the algorithm per master key (one for SRTP, one for SRTCP), and each packet is processed by a single invocation.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the call shares one secret key. From it, each side makes its own lock settings for media packets and for control packets.

sections.title: How AEAD and Counter Mode Are Used
sections.content:
Every packet is split into three kinds of data. Associated Data is authenticated but not encrypted. Plaintext is both encrypted and authenticated. Raw Data is neither. Encryption takes the key (16 or 32 octets), a 12-octet IV, the Associated Data and the Plaintext, and returns a ciphertext that is longer than the Plaintext by exactly the tag length, with the tag appended.

On receipt, all incoming packets MUST pass AEAD authentication before anything else happens. Plaintext and Associated Data MUST NOT be released, and the ciphertext MUST NOT be decrypted, until the tag has been validated. An invalid packet is discarded and a Validation Error flag is raised; how that flag is handled is local policy.

In counter mode, the 12-octet IV plus a 4-octet block counter is fed to AES. The first 16-octet block is saved for forming the tag, and the rest of the keystream is XORed with the Plaintext. In theory this allows up to 2^36 - 32 octets per packet. If the same IV and key are ever used twice, the keystream repeats, and for GCM this compromises the integrity mechanism for all future uses of that key.

Because AEAD already authenticates, the older SRTP and SRTCP authentication tags SHOULD NOT be present and are NOT RECOMMENDED. This contradicts the SRTCP tag requirement in Section 3.4 of RFC 3711, which the RFC accepts. The field is retained mainly for applications such as RFC 4771 that use it to carry extra information. RTP padding is RECOMMENDED not to be used unless needed to disguise the Plaintext length.
sections.eli5: Some of a packet is put in the locked box, some is left visible but sealed so you can see it was not changed, and some is just tacked on outside. The receiver checks the seal first and only opens the box if the seal is good.

sections.title: AES-GCM Processing for SRTP
sections.content:
The 12-octet SRTP IV is built by concatenating 2 octets of zeroes, the 4-octet SSRC, the 4-octet rollover counter (ROC) and the 2-octet sequence number (SEQ), then XORing that value with the 12-octet encryption salt.

All SRTP packets MUST be both authenticated and encrypted. The RTP header fields (version, padding flag, extension flag, CSRC count, marker, payload type, sequence number, timestamp, SSRC, optional CSRC identifiers and the optional extension) are Associated Data. The payload, any RTP padding and the pad count are Plaintext. The optional MKI and the not-recommended SRTP authentication tag are Raw Data added after encryption. The resulting ciphertext replaces the payload, with the tag at its end, immediately before the MKI. Even an empty payload is still processed, leaving just the tag.

Header extensions are Associated Data whether or not they were encrypted under RFC 6904. When RFC 6904 is used, their keystream MUST come from the AES Counter Mode transform for AEAD_AES_128_GCM and the AES_256_CM transform for AEAD_AES_256_GCM, and the originator must do that encryption before invoking AEAD.

The (ROC, SEQ, SSRC) triple must never repeat under one master key. A rekey MUST happen before (ROC, SEQ) cycles back. Each originating endpoint MUST draw SSRC values only from its own pool, keep a history of values issued under the current key, and never reissue one. A rekey MUST also happen before a pool runs out, and SSRC signaling MUST be integrity protected. For GCM with shared master keys, an SSRC collision MUST be prevented from happening even once.
sections.eli5: Every packet gets its own one-time lock setting, mixed from who is sending it and which packet number it is. The rules make sure two packets never share a setting, because that would let a thief break the locks.

sections.title: AES-GCM Processing for SRTCP
sections.content:
All SRTCP compound packets MUST be authenticated, but encryption is optional. The sender chooses per packet and signals the choice with a 1-bit Encryption flag placed just before the 31-bit SRTCP index.

The SRTCP IV is formed from 2 octets of zeroes, the 4-octet SSRC, 2 octets of zeroes, a single 0 bit and the 31-bit SRTCP index, and the result is XORed with the 12-octet salt.

When the flag is 1, the first RTCP header words, SSRC, Encryption flag and SRTCP index are Associated Data, the rest is Plaintext, and the cipher (with its tag) goes just before the flag and index. When the flag is 0, there is no Plaintext and everything except the MKI and optional tag is Associated Data. AEAD still runs and returns a field exactly the tag length, placed before the flag and index.

A new master key MUST be established before the 31-bit SRTCP index cycles back to its original value, ideally well before. The SSRC management rules from the SRTP section also apply.
sections.eli5: Control messages always get a seal, but putting them in the locked box is the sender's choice. A small flag tells the receiver which was done.

sections.title: Required Parameters and Suites
sections.content:
Any AEAD algorithm used with SRTP and SRTCP must meet five constraints: the maximum Associated Data length must be at least 12 octets, the minimum and maximum nonce length must both be 12 octets, and for GCM the maximum Plaintext per invocation must be at most 2^36 - 32 octets and the maximum ciphertext at most 2^36 - 16 octets. The tag MUST be 16 octets, an instantiation may be invoked at most 2^48 times for SRTP and 2^31 times for SRTCP, and for GCM the block counter MUST be 32 bits.

For key derivation, AEAD_AES_128_GCM MUST use the 128-bit AES_CM PRF from RFC 3711, and AEAD_AES_256_GCM MUST use the AES_256_CM_PRF from RFC 6188. Any implementation of AES-GCM SRTP MUST support both algorithms. Both suites use a 96-bit master salt and a 128-bit tag.
sections.eli5: There are two sizes of lock, a medium one and a big one. Both must be able to handle the same size of key-mixing pieces and always carry a full-sized seal.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Secrets must be handled carefully. A secret master salt MUST be erased when no longer needed, and the master key and all keys derived from it MUST be kept secret and erased when done.

The Block Counter MUST be reset to 1 at the start of each packet and MUST NOT exceed 2^32 - 1 for GCM. IV uniqueness still holds because the IV includes SSRC, ROC and SEQ, or the SRTCP index. Each time a rekey occurs, the starting values of the 31-bit SRTCP index and the 48-bit SRTP packet index (ROC||SEQ) MUST be saved. Processing MUST stop if either index cycles back to its initial value, and MUST NOT resume until a new session with a new master key is set up.

On tag size, the authors and the working group considered the risks of truncated AES-GCM tags too high, so the 16-octet tag is required to effectively eliminate the risk of an attacker inserting fraudulent data.
sections.eli5: Never reuse the same lock setting, and always change to a brand-new key before the packet counters run all the way around.

sections.title: Registrations for SDES, DTLS-SRTP and MIKEY
sections.content:
For Security Descriptions (SDES, RFC 4568), IANA registered the crypto suites AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM.

For DTLS-SRTP (RFC 5764), IANA registered two SRTP protection profiles: SRTP_AEAD_AES_128_GCM as {0x00, 0x07} and SRTP_AEAD_AES_256_GCM as {0x00, 0x08}. Both have no separate authentication function, key or tag, since AEAD supplies the tag.

For MIKEY (RFC 3830), the RFC adds type 20, AEAD authentication tag length with value 16 octets, and the encryption algorithm AES-GCM as value 6. MIKEY specifies the key length and tag length separately from the algorithm family, so the three together select the AEAD algorithm. Because the KDF is restricted, the SRTP PRF must be AES-CM whenever an AEAD algorithm is used, and the AES_256_CM_PRF follows for AEAD_AES_256_GCM.
sections.eli5: Each way of setting up a call has a list of cipher names. This RFC got the two new ciphers added to each list so the systems can agree on them.

items.title: Associated Data
items.text: Authenticated but not encrypted, such as the RTP header fields.

items.title: Plaintext
items.text: Encrypted and authenticated, such as the RTP payload.

items.title: Raw Data
items.text: Neither, added after encryption, such as the optional MKI.
